The geometry of

Research directions

Competing objectives

Cover the range of useful trade-offs.

Equal steps in a preference weight can leave gaps on the Pareto front. I study how the front’s geometry can guide the choice of weights.

Model trade-offs

Same front. Different coverage.

Choosing an LLM summarizer. Each candidate balances summary quality and factual faithfulness. Each point is a different balance between these goals.

Higher scores are better. Click a point to explore a candidate.

Even weight steps can leave gaps between choices.

Illustrative normalized scores. SURF studies quality and faithfulness rewards in LLM summarization. See the paper’s application.

SURF · Cover the Pareto front evenlySample scalarization weights using the geometry of the trade-off curve.NeurIPS 2026
Nested decisions

Optimize a decision through another problem.

In bilevel optimization, an outer decision changes an optimized inner response. I study how curvature, update rules, and moving constraints affect the cost of learning.

Price and response

The bakery sets a price. The customer responds.

🧑‍🍳
BakerySets the price, x
🛍️
CustomerChooses bread, y

The shop wants profit. The customer wants a purchase that is worth the price.

$3.00

Add optional constraints

No extra constraints.

🥖Customer buys, y*(x)5 kg
💰Bakery profit$10.00

At $3 per kg, the customer buys 5 kg. The bakery earns $10.

The bakery chooses x. The customer determines y, so the bakery’s profit follows the response curve.

About this illustrative model

Without extra limits, the customer prefers 8 − x kg. This maximizes their modeled satisfaction minus the price paid. Bread costs the shop $1 per kg, so profit is (x − 1)y.

A budget limits spending: xy ≤ 12. Stock limits the amount bought: y ≤ 3.

Learning & behavior

Speech models and LLM agents.

My application work develops training targets for speech models and studies the timing and memory of LLM agents’ decisions.

About

Liuyuan Jiang

I am a PhD student in Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Rochester, advised by Prof. Lisha Chen. Previously, I was a PhD student at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, advised by Prof. Tianyi Chen.

I study how optimization shapes learning: navigating competing objectives, solving nested problems, and understanding model behavior.
